current_answer: An open vLLM-Omni Self-Forcing PR streams video in chunks and accepts mid-stream text prompts. On one A800 80 GB, its first nine frames arrived in 1.80 seconds, but 81 frames took 10.57 seconds to generate about 5.06 seconds of 16-fps video. Later chunks also took longer than their playout time. It is not a merged, sustained live service. A recent H3 decoder improves another stage, not prompt-to-viewer response. Receiver delay, accepted quality and full cost remain unknown.

catalogue_card.question: Can one GPU stream interactive AI video without falling behind?
catalogue_card.text: An open Self-Forcing PR sent its first nine frames in 1.8 seconds on one A800 80 GB. Its 81-frame WebSocket run took 10.57 seconds for 5.06 seconds of playback. Incremental output is real; a sustained viewer session is not yet shown.

summary: An open vLLM-Omni PR proposes Self-Forcing text-to-video over stepwise WebSocket with prompt updates. On one eager A800 80 GB at 832×480/16 fps, the author reports nine frames at 1.80 seconds, later 12-frame chunks in 1.16–1.74 seconds each, and 81 frames in 10.57 seconds. The 81 frames play for 5.06 seconds. No remote receiver, merged release, accepted quality or full bill is reported.

SolarX-Team released a causal H3 VAE decoder on 16 October. It reports the first decoded frame 0.04 seconds after the first latent exists, versus an official decoder that waits for seven latents then decodes its first window in 0.73 seconds. On 30 MCL-JCV clips, source-reconstruction PSNR is 30.41 dB versus official 31.04 dB. SolarWM generates five-latent chunks; receiver-visible response and cost are unmeasured.

ComfyStreamerH3 reports a warm RTX 5090 paired job: two 15.08-second 448×256 clips in a median 23.51 seconds across 11 jobs. The HLS demo waits for two completed MP4s before playback and queues prompt changes behind the current clip. Its managed example instead selects RTX PRO 6000, listed at $4.54/hour before plan and storage. Receiver response, accepted quality and delivered-hour cost are unknown.

StreamForce releases a browser force-control route. Its local headless-viewer test put an unpaced force change 213 frames ahead of display (about 13 seconds at 16 FPS), versus six frames (0.4 seconds) of steady-state queue lead with pacing. One H200 reached about 23 generated FPS in the newer demo; quality reportedly drifts beyond roughly 10–15 seconds. Remote control-to-visible time and full cost are unknown.

AWS Labs reports a browser-playable Waypoint-1.5 route on one H100 or A10G. The 82/25 FPS figures are local generation rates; one remote sample delivered 44.6 FPS. Cold compilation took 645 seconds and the scene visibly decayed after roughly 512 generated frames. A costed, stable hour is untested.

StreamRender-H3 reports a same-rack eight-GB200 browser racing route. Its 218 ms warm diffusion step, 295.58 ms median GPU RGB interval and ~1.03-second browser publication interval are different clocks; control-to-visible latency, wider scene fit and cost remain unknown.

TeleFuser reports a four-H100 LingBot-World v2 LiveKit route: a later one-minute replay generated 59.75 seconds of media in 79.2523 seconds of session time, with first client frame at 5.9822 seconds. This is separate from a 77-frame 17.1399-FPS target-compute gate and separate from its H3 service route.

Scope documents WebRTC video input/output and live prompt changes. One Thailand event operator reports about ten minutes cold remote-beta H100 readiness and distinct 512×512 LongLive T2V versus StreamDiffusionV2 V2V results. Paid-use rights, venue delay, session rollover and complete cost remain unverified.

Hallo-Live authors report 20.38 generated FPS and 0.94-second model latency for text-to-audio-video on two H200s. The released inference command saves a final 24-fps MP4, above the paper throughput, while a maintainer estimates about 60 GB default peak VRAM; a 24-GB route is theoretical. No receiver-visible conversation or complete bill is documented.

LiveAvatar authors report 45.2 generated FPS and 1.21 seconds from audio arrival to first visual output for a four-step FP8, 720×400, five-H100 audio-driven avatar path. Their paper estimates roughly three seconds end to end with transport and says this is not seamless two-way interaction. The released one-GPU route is offline; an independent one-H200 cold job took 181.44 seconds to produce a short final clip.

ShotStream reports 15.95 generated FPS at 832×480 on one H200 for a Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B-based multi-shot model. Its public inference example reads a prepared CSV and writes a final 16-FPS MP4; it does not demonstrate live viewer delivery or in-session prompt changes.

Veda-on-ComfyUI project test: on an RTX 5070 12 GB, a 124-frame 1344×768 H3 T2VA clip took 342.1 seconds with default attention, 230.9 with SageAttention and 130.1 with Veda. The 7.1× number is attention-only; the full-job default-to-Veda ratio is 2.63×.

RAVEN ComfyUI’s 192-frame T2VA test used an H200 constrained to 24.100 GiB free and synthetic conditioning. It sampled eight seconds in 301.30 seconds, with first local fragment at 51.46 seconds. A separate 39-frame real-prompt test used unconstrained H200 VRAM; neither proves full-size real-prompt generation on a physical 24-GiB card.

Tavus describes Griffin-Lite as a full-duplex 720p conversational-video preview. Its reported 320 ms chunks and 0.43 s audio-to-video generator latency are not a customer session; NVIDIA VideoFDB has separate 1,892/2,232 ms median generation/perception timing.

vLLM-Omni merged request-scoped H3 latent-mask editing into its video API on 20 September. Source video/audio and masks can preserve or regenerate regions in a completed job. Its proposed ComfyUI editing node and raw-mask server follow-up remained open at the 4 October check; the pool has not run this route.

An independent project reports a warm FastH3 Preview v1 14.375-second 1344×768/24 fps audio-video clip saved in 13.506 seconds on eight H100 80 GB GPUs. A separate matched eight-H200 stock-versus-patched test reports 23.810 to 14.085 seconds; do not merge those comparisons. No accepted-quality, cold-start, receiver or cost result is available.

TaoMate-H3 reports 14.810 seconds pure DiT and 17.287 seconds to benchmark first playable video for a ten-second 480×864 T2AV job on eight H20 96 GB GPUs. First playable includes video VAE decode and H.264 publication but excludes internal audio preparation. Current CLI output is a final MP4; sustained viewer delivery is unmeasured.

NVIDIA Sol-H3 reports eight-B300 warm medians of 1.653/3.732/6.612 seconds for nominal 5/10/15-second 1344×768 T2VA outputs with audio. Final MP4 encoding, load, and compilation are excluded; continuous streaming and in-session control remain future work. The 11.04× five-second comparison also changes Base H3 from 49 denoiser forwards to a four-forward FastH3 adapter.

Vidu S2-Editing documents a source-fed live editing path: publish video into RTC, subscribe to edited RTC output, and optionally relay it to RTMP. It bills one credit per live second; at a $0.005 standard credit, 3,600 billed seconds imply $18 before delivery costs. No independent viewer-delay or long-session result is available.

vLLM-Omni’s current recipe reports a separate warmed eight-B300 FastH3 Dense T2VA test: a 4.4-second, 1344×768 clip returned as a complete MP4 in 11.7 and 11.8 seconds. Four denoiser evaluations took 2.36–2.37 seconds, so the complete short-clip response was still slower than playback. This is distinct from the previously reported longer FastH3 profile that beat its playback clock.

vLLM-Omni v0.30.0 documents opt-in Ref2VA long-video continuation. Its maintainer reports one 736-frame, 30.667-second original-H3 output on eight B300 GPUs at 1344×768, 24 fps, 50 steps; full wall time and live delivery are not supplied.

Comfy Org reports that the H3 video VAE encode/decode round trip fell from 24.3 to 12.7 seconds on an RTX 5090 at 1344×768, 129 frames after its v0.36.0 update. This is one stage, not whole-job speed.

vLLM-Omni says H3 can admit and retire requests between denoise steps, but its stated two-H100 test with four simultaneous 672×384, 209-frame, 30-step requests reports worse wall time and mean latency under four-way co-batching than ordinary request mode.
The source says staggered-arrival behavior remains unmeasured. The benchmark does not predict two RTX 5090 GPUs, a different job shape, a FastH3 adapter, a browser-visible result, or a public stream.

The current two-RTX-5090 DLO launch selects the FL2VA DiT; T2VA uses that path. The source recommends a 384 GiB host, while its one 50-step T2VA validation returned 124 1344×768 / 24 fps frames in 8 minutes 38 seconds.
vLLM-Omni’s current ComfyUI client still accepts one FL2VA frame even though the server recipe can represent ordered first-and-last-frame inputs.
uncertainty: Self-Forcing stepwise support is an open contributor PR; one A800 local test did not sustain unbuffered 16-fps playout or measure a remote viewer.
The reported 40 ms starts after latent generation; the optimized decode benchmark does not name the GPU, and no integrated viewer test or bill is published.
ComfyStreamerH3’s warm 1.28× playback-duration ratio is not a measured browser response or accepted-session result.
StreamForce numbers are project-maintained and not pool-reproduced; paper and current demo benchmark different implementations.
The six-frame figure is a local headless-viewer queue position, not measured remote input-to-visible latency or guaranteed p95.
Longer coherent play, full GPU/transport cost and independent user acceptance remain unknown.
First-party pool analytics remain unavailable; attention, repeat use and funding are unknown.
Waypoint measurements and browser validation are project reports; raw captures are held outside its repository and this pool did not deploy it.
The 82/25 FPS figures are instance-local generation rates, not remote delivery. One path’s 263 ms lag does not establish p95 or other regions.
Scene coherence, secure transport, reconnect and full billed-hour performance remain unverified for a production session.
First-party analytics remain unavailable; attention, repeat use and funding are unknown.
StreamRender-H3 timings and browser integration are project-reported; the pool has not operated the eight-GB200 runtime.
The 1.03-second figure is a browser publication interval, not input-to-screen latency; sustained p95 delay and remote-network behavior are unknown.
The published racing-trained renderer has not been validated for other games, camera views, accepted quality, one-hour operation, or cost.
H3 Community License terms require use-specific review before commercial operation.
First-party pool analytics remain unavailable; attention, repeat use and funding are unknown.
TeleFuser timing is a project-maintained one-run report, not pool-reproduced; no one-hour receiver continuity, control-to-visible delay, accepted quality or full bill is established.
Scope has not been run by this pool; the event record is one self-report and its possible connected-idle charge is not a settled rate.
Hallo-Live paper timings and memory are not pool-reproduced; public code lacks a documented live receiver and 24-GB default route.
LiveAvatar paper and repository use different H100/H800 labels for the headline hardware; use the five-H100 paper measurement as written, not an interchangeable H800 or 48GB result.
The independent one-H200 result is a cold offline job, not a five-card warm stream or delivered-hour bill. No pool receiver session, consented quality test or full invoice exists.
ShotStream H200 throughput is paper-reported and not pool-reproduced; the released example does not measure prompt-to-visible latency, sustained receiver delivery, accepted quality or operating cost.
The Veda benchmark is project-maintained on a specific RTX 5070 T2VA setup; 5090, 3060, reference-input and longer-output quality and complete-job gains are unverified by this pool.
RAVEN physical 24-GiB real-prompt 192-frame fit, viewer delivery, accepted quality and usable cost are unmeasured; maintainer advises 160 GiB available host RAM.
Griffin-Lite is limited to selected research testers; no pool-operated session, Griffin-specific customer price, accepted-quality distribution or delivered-hour bill exists.
The merged H3 mask API has no pool-operated edit, accepted-quality comparison, complete wait, bill, or live receiver result. The client and raw-mask PR states may change after 4 October.

The Hopper FastH3 results are project-reported. Warm complete-MP4 timing excludes load and compilation; quality suite, receiver-visible continuity, retries and billing are unknown. The H100 headline and H200 A/B use different hardware.

TaoMate-H3 figures are project-reported for one eight-H20 480×864 test. No pool test, cold start, internal audio preparation, receiver-visible first frame, repeated-block timing, accepted quality or delivered-hour cost is available.
The one-RTX-5090 converted TaoMate LoRA is a separate self-reported ComfyUI offline path, not validation of the official chunked runtime.
Sol-H3 results are project-reported, not pool-tested; final encoded-to-viewer time, quality acceptance, queue behavior, session reliability and cost are unknown.
Vidu S2 Editing topology and billing are provider-documented; no pool or independent timed RTC-to-RTMP session, billed invoice, viewer latency, or long-run reliability record was found.

The new FastH3 Dense timing is two project-reported warm runs on eight B300 GPUs for one 4.4-second T2VA shape; no pool reproduction, cost, video-quality, queue, first-frame, or viewer result is available.
The vLLM-Omni long-video example is a project-maintained eight-B300 result. The 300-second request cap does not validate five-minute output, acceptable joins, cost, or a stream.

The ComfyUI VAE speed figures are provider-maintained node-level A/B measurements on one RTX 5090 setup. Full H3 render time, quality under a pinned workflow, repeated-run reliability, and cost impact remain unmeasured.
The batching result is one project-maintained two-H100 benchmark with four simultaneous requests. Staggered arrivals, other job shapes, other hardware, and viewer-visible behavior remain unmeasured.
The documented two-RTX-5090 result is one project-published T2VA validation. The pool did not independently audit its environment, media, timing, or quality.

The two-5090 command selects the FL2VA path; it does not establish a combined multi-task service, Ref2VA, a two-keyframe client workflow, warm performance, streaming, queueing, or first visible frame.
vLLM-Omni’s current ComfyUI client-scope statements come from an open RFC. The pool did not install or test the server or client.
Dreamverse’s FastH3 profile is project documentation; the pool did not install or run it, inspect a generated handoff, or measure buffer, cost, recovery, or uptime.
FastVideo and ComfyUI still conflict on FastH3 8-Step V2 FL2VA scope. The pool did not run a pinned T2VA or FL2VA workflow.
No pool test, invoice, uptime log, end-to-end source-to-visible latency measurement, or first-party pool analytics record is available.
